compression.title: AI Incident Database
compression.lede: is an editor-resolved database of AI harm events, run by the Responsible AI Collaborative (MMRS record; its home page), "dedicated to indexing the collective history of harms or near harms": its unit the incident, reports attached, each with a citation page at /cite/N.

sentences.text: The AI Incident Database (AIID) is an editor-resolved database of AI harm events (MMRS record), "dedicated to indexing the collective history of harms or near harms realized in the real world by the deployment of artificial intelligence systems" in its home page's words, which the MMRS record quotes and the OECD's catalogue repeats as a "free and open-source project", and which Paeth and colleagues (AAAI-25) describe as a project that catalogs AI incidents and provides a platform to classify them for operational and research goals.

Its unit is the incident, with the reports that document it attached, and every incident has a stable citation page at incidentdatabase.ai/cite/N (MMRS record); the Editor's Guide defines the incident as "an alleged harm or near harm event to people, property, or the environment where an AI system is implicated" and the report as a source document attached to an incident ID, several of which may document one event, and the MMRS record quotes the definition and adds that reports may be news articles, papers or posts.

Its home page sets it beside "similar databases in aviation and computer security", to learn from experience and prevent or mitigate bad outcomes; McGregor's founding paper starts from mature industrial sectors such as aviation that collect their failures in incident databases, while intelligent systems "cause real world harms without a collective memory of their failings"; the about page invokes the transportation sector (FAA and FARS) and computer systems, the research page "Defining an AI Incident" takes aviation's distinction of an accident (substantial damage or loss of life) from an incident (the risk of an accident substantially increased), and Partnership on AI's workstream page places it among safety-critical systems in transportation, healthcare and energy, a crowdsourced central repository of more than 1,200 reports.

Sean McGregor's founding paper, submitted to arXiv on 17 November 2020, describes "an incident collection initiated by an industrial/non-profit cooperative", searchable by facet and full text over more than 1,000 incident reports, and on 18 November 2020 he introduced it on Partnership on AI's site as "a systematized collection of incidents where intelligent systems have caused safety, fairness, or other real-world problems" (the introduction quoted in Wikipedia's reference); the snapshots page asks that the database as a whole be cited by his IAAI-21 paper, and the MMRS record dates the founding to 2020 as the arXiv paper describes it, with more than 1,000 reports at launch.

The home and about pages call it "a project of the Responsible AI Collaborative, an organization chartered to advance the AI Incident Database"; the OECD's catalogue entry (uploaded 25 April 2024) names the Collaborative as developing organisation and MIT's tracker credits it with creating and maintaining the database; the about page credits Sean McGregor with launching it and names him Executive Director, heads a logo block "Database Founding Sponsor" whose image the page labels Partnership on AI, and records that two people contributed to its early stages through their roles with the Partnership on AI; the MMRS record gives the same operator, founder, director and founding sponsor.

Wikipedia has no article of its own for it: "AI Incident Database" redirects, with no section anchor, to Partnership on AI (a redirect from a subtopic, with possibilities), whose article records that Partnership on AI announced it in November 2020 as "a tool to identify, assess, manage, and communicate AI risk and harm", that Partnership on AI's response to NIST presented it as meeting attributes of the AI Risk Management Framework, that it was among the Safety Critical AI program's initiatives, and, under programs and initiatives, that it "shifted to a new special-purpose independent non-profit in 2022", the non-profit unnamed; the article is tagged for primary sources (April 2025) and as AI-generated (October 2025).
The MMRS record has the database run by the Responsible AI Collaborative since 2020, and Wikipedia has it shift to an independent non-profit in 2022; the two dates stand each with its source.

The Editor's Guide (Version 2, 1 October 2026, by Daniel Atherton and Sean McGregor, drafted with disclosed generative-AI assistance) keeps the incident apart from the AI issue, "an alleged harm or near harm by an AI system that has yet to occur or be detected", from the incident ID, the editorial record that bounds and summarizes an event, and from the report: "A report is evidence; an incident ID is the database’s normalized account of an event", so that a later source on the same event is usually an additional report, not a new incident.

A variant is, in the guide, "a distinct incident involving the same intelligent system, substantially similar causative factors, and substantially similar harms as a known incident", as the MMRS record restates it; the incident page for 693 describes the variant as having the same causes, harms and system, grouped under the first reported incident, and adds that variants "do not need to have been reported outside the AIID".

The Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that at the database's name Google's AI Overview gave neither the incident as the unit, nor the reports attached to it, nor the citation page /cite/N, "collects public and crowdsourced reports" standing in for the unit, and that at the question of what counts the incident, the issue and the variant were the guide's definitions in substance, the first verbatim, and the report was again not stated; the MMRS record's negative tags hold that it is not a list of research papers, its unit the event and papers entering as reports.

A candidate passes the guide's five-question test: a specific event, an identifiable AI system, a causal implication (an important role in the chain of events, not necessarily the sole or dominant cause), harm or credible near harm (a chain that could readily have produced harm, stopped by an external factor independent of the system and not a built-in safeguard functioning as designed), and adequate evidence, at least one source supporting the essential event (guide); the MMRS record states the same test and records that admission requires harm or credible near harm.

At "what counts as an incident in the ai incident database" the Overview read the guide and kept its distinctions with one compression, the five-part test given as three thresholds, the identifiable system folded into "AI implication" and adequate evidence dropped, so that the composition carried the test's harm condition and lost its evidence condition, the condition on which the MMRS record's account of what its selection leaves out rests (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The research page "Defining an AI Incident" calls the criteria adaptive, reports "accepted or rejected on the basis of a growing rule set defined in the Editor's Guide"; the about page asks that an event be submitted when in doubt, the project meant to converge on shared criteria through the community's candidates, and says its initial set of more than 1,000 incident reports was intentionally broad, an autonomous car killing a pedestrian among its examples; the guide's presumptive exclusions include general criticism of a product or technology class without identified harm and benchmark failures, model errors or hallucinations that remain inside testing or private drafting, "presumptions rather than absolute prohibitions", which the MMRS record quotes as "benchmark failures that stay in testing" and "general criticism of a technology".

Anyone may submit (MMRS record; the home page invites incident reports, to be indexed and made discoverable), and the incident editors, Daniel Atherton the lead, resolve submissions and maintain them; the database is managed in a participatory manner by those contributing code, research and broader impacts, CSET and Nikiforos Pittaras (GMF) have contributed its taxonomies (about page), MIT's tracker credits the Collaborative with reviewing all submitted reports, and the MMRS record's intake field states open submission with editors resolving submissions and maintaining records.

Every incident has a suggested citation crediting its submitters and editors, at incidentdatabase.ai/cite/N (snapshots page); that citation page per incident is the model the MMRS meta-aggregator follows, and the MMRS record observes per item the incident id and citation page, title, date, alleged deployer and developer, harmed parties, attached reports, CSET and GMF classifications and variants.

A duplicate is merged into the earlier record and its citation page stays up and points there (MMRS record): the citation record for 637 reads "This incident is a duplicate of Incident 112", its reports migrated, as the guide's duplicate mapping redirects a retired identifier to its canonical record; ids therefore include merged duplicates, and the highest id seen, 1788 (MMRS record, 2026-10-28; the home page on 2026-10-29), is an upper bound on incidents, against which Paeth and colleagues counted over 750 distinct incidents detailed by more than 3000 indexed third-party reports at their writing.

The whole database is offered as weekly point-in-time dumps in JSON, MongoDB archive and CSV, listed from 29 March 2021 to 26 October 2026, with a weekly Excel export of numbered incidents and their taxonomy classifications (snapshots page; MMRS record, which counts the weekly snapshots as its version history); the guide warns that the live site can change after an export is created.

The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity it describes, each assertion with a source and a basis (operator statement, third-party report, observation, reading) and the lifecycle (active) apart from the observation that saw it (2026-10-28), and it leaves the Wikidata item and any data licence beyond the snapshots page unchecked.

The OECD's catalogue gives its usage rights as open source/permissive and its licence as Apache 2.0, without saying of what; the MMRS record observes the code open source and no data licence stated on the snapshots page, and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that the Overview's "free, open-source" does not distinguish the two.

The guide's governing principle is that the database "records publicly documented allegations of harm or near harm" and "does not independently adjudicate every factual claim"; it is "a curated archive of publicly documented incidents, issues, reports, and responses", not a neutral mirror of all AI harms, a comprehensive denominator for risk rates or an independent adjudication of every event; wealthy countries, prominent companies, spectacular events and English-language reporting are likely overrepresented, and harms to marginalized groups, inside private organizations or in ordinary administration may be underrepresented; and "A lack of records is not evidence that a sector or country has no incidents."

Paeth and colleagues find that certain patterns of incidents present structural ambiguities that challenge incident databasing and that epistemic uncertainty in incident reporting is unavoidable; MIT's tracker states that, the reporting being voluntary, its input is subject to some sampling bias, and that a systematic validation study of its classifications has not yet been completed.

On the MMRS record's reading a measured study enters as a report when it documents an event, and what an answer surface does with a source on an ordinary day, with no harm event, has no unit: attribution erasure, citation fidelity and provenance stripping enter when they attach to a harm, so the database has no field for attribution, and whether the reports' texts are archived beyond their links the record leaves unknown.

The archive's Hexagonal Lexical Engine (#543, 10 March 2026) lists AI ethics glossaries, "AIAAIC, AI Incident DB", among the venues to which it addresses definitions with citations of three of its terms: semantic liquidation, ghost governance and taxonomic violence.

Incident 693, "Google AI Reportedly Delivering Confidently Incorrect and Harmful Information", dated 2024-05-14 and edited by Daniel Atherton, alleges that Google developed and deployed the system and that Google users and the general public were harmed, carries reports naming Google's AI Overviews, and is machine-classified under MIT's taxonomy as false or misleading information (incident page); the MMRS record calls it the field's index case in the database, holding it with seven reports and the AI Overviews launch errors.

MIT's AI Incident Tracker classifies 1,600 incidents from the database by risk, cause, harm, severity and other dimensions, its raw reports processed by Arcola AI's LLM pipeline against the MIT Risk Repository and a severity scale based on CSET's AI Harm Taxonomy (tracker page); the MMRS record lists the tracker as classifying AIID reports, and the MIT AI Risk Repository as aggregating risk frameworks over the same ground with its own incident tracker.

In the harm basin, where the MMRS record gives it the roles of harm and monitoring, its neighbours are the OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor, automated and news-derived (MMRS record; incident 693's page describes it as collecting and classifying incidents and hazards in real time from news sources), and the AIAAIC Repository; it is neither the OECD monitor nor a vulnerability database (MMRS record).

The Kaggle dataset "AI Incidents, Failures & Controversies Database" (32 incidents, 29 companies, 13 countries, 24 columns, CC BY-SA 4.0), which takes primary incident records and AIID identifiers from the database and cites Stanford HAI's AI Index 2025 for a 56.4% surge in AI incidents in 2024, is another dataset with a near name (MMRS record), and at the database's name the Overview did not use it, its card beside the database's own (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The rails at the two addresses also carry an ACM paper read only by its snippet (submissions of incidents and controversies included by criteria such as relevance, fairness and accuracy), two TIME clips on LinkedIn titled "AI Incident Database | TIME posted on the topic" and "AI Incidents Rise 50% Year-Over-Year: AI Incident Database", and two YouTube videos admitted by title, "Examples of AI real attacks" and "Establishing Effective Serious Incident Reporting Frameworks – Jimmy Farrell | IASEAI 2025".

At its name the Overview composed the database at the grain of its own about page and kept it apart from its neighbours, giving the operator, the aviation model and the MIT tracker as a derived layer, which are the MMRS record's fields, and omitting the incident-and-report structure that makes the database what it is; no card was machinemediation.org, the meta-aggregator's record not yet indexed (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), whose battery asks that the operator be named, the unit stated with reports attached, the database not merged with the OECD monitor or the AIAAIC, and the citation page given (MMRS record).
